2610.27055.title: Planets surviving common envelope evolution should be rare, massive, and orbit very close to their host star

figures.caption: Figure 1: Summary of the steps in our simulation process. We include an approximate timeline of when the conditions for the common envelope can occur along the host star’s evolution. The main parameters we compare to determine if a planet undergoes CE are the stellar radius ($R_{\star}$) and the star’s Roche radius ($R_{Roche}$). We present the termination and survival conditions for planets that reach the final semi-major axis ($a_{f}$) after CE.

Figure 3: Evolution of variable tidal Q factors for a $2M_{\odot}$ host star. The light blue lines show the evolution of $Q^{\prime}_{\star}$ (solid) and $Q^{\prime}_{p}$ (dotted) for a planet that survives CE evolution. Critical stages of stellar evolution are labeled and shaded in gray.

Figure 5: The planet semi-major axis evolution color-coded by scenario outcome for the case with static $Q^{\prime}_{\mathrm{{\star,p}}}$ and $\alpha$=2. 
Inset: Zoom-in of the same plot centered around the final stages of the planet. The surviving planet ends up on a very close orbit, while the accreted case is destroyed within the host star. In the case where the planet never enters CE, tidal evolution causes the planet to migrate into a wider orbit as the star loses mass at the end of the giant phase.

Figure 6: Final distributions of planets surviving CE evolution in the illustrative case (2 $M_{\odot}$, static $Q^{\prime}_{\star}=10^{5}$ and $Q^{\prime}_{\mathrm{p}}=10^{5.5}$, $\alpha$=2). Our results show that planets surviving CE are massive and will evolve to very short orbits. The bimodality in semi-major axis and the spike in planet mass is due to planets surviving at two different points in stellar evolution corresponding to two different radii of their host star during the AGB stage.

Figure 7: Initial planet mass vs semi-major axis of the population around a 2 $M_{\odot}$ main-sequence host, run with static $Q^{\prime}_{\star}=10^{5}$ and $Q^{\prime}_{\mathrm{p}}=10^{5.5}$, $\alpha$=2 (illustrative case), and zoomed in around this area of interest. Each point is color-coded by outcome after the common envelope. Surviving planets are highlighted in light blue.
Planets that survive common envelope evolution tend to be massive ($\gtrsim 10M_{\rm{Jup}}$) and orbit in a narrow range of semi-major axes near the boundary between planets that are tidally disrupted within the star and accreted onto the cores and planets that move outwards and never experience engulfment.

Figure 8: Final semi-major axis of the surviving planets in our illustrative case (2 $M_{\odot}$, static $Q^{\prime}_{\star}=10^{5}$ and $Q^{\prime}_{\mathrm{p}}=10^{5.5}$, $\alpha$=2). The results are shown relative to the evaporation limit (top) and the tidal disruption limit (bottom). Planets that survive the CE phase typically have semi-major axes just beyond the evaporation or disruption limit (within a factor of 2 of each limit).

Figure 9: Joint distribution of planet mass vs final semi-major axis scatter plot shown for planets that survive CE around a 1 and 2 $M_{\odot}$ main sequence hosts. We also show 1D histograms of planet mass and semi-major axis in the panels above and to the right of the main figure. The two sets of simulations we compare both used a static $Q^{\prime}_{\star}=10^{5}$ and $Q^{\prime}_{\mathrm{p}}=10^{5.5}$ and common envelope efficiency $\alpha=2.5$. We also plot the semi-major axis and mass of WD 1856b [61] and the candidate WD 0310b [33] in square markers for comparison. The inferred masses and orbital distances of these two objects fall well outside the typical distributions of planets surviving CE under these assumptions.

Figure 10: Final white dwarf mass distributions of systems with CE survivors around a 1 $M_{\odot}$ (left) and 2 $M_{\odot}$ (right) progenitors with a static $Q^{\prime}_{\star}=10^{5}$ and $Q^{\prime}_{\mathrm{p}}=10^{5.5}$ and color-coded by for two values of $\alpha$. We mark (green dashed lines) the typical mass of a WD that would result from each progenitor mass if the system did not go through CE. We also note the stellar evolution phase that corresponds to each feature in the distributions. For the 1 $M_{\odot}$ host, CE occurs during the RGB phase and leaves behind less massive WDs. For the 2 $M_{\odot}$ host, CE happens mostly during the AGB phase and result in slightly more massive WDs (with the exception of the $\alpha=20$ case which can have survivors during the RGB phase as well).

2610.27055.abstract: The discovery of exoplanets around white dwarfs uniquely informs our understanding of planetary survival through stellar evolution. Common Envelope (CE) evolution is one of the proposed mechanisms that could shape the orbital architecture of these planets around stellar remnants. In this work, we predict the occurrence rate and orbital separation/planet mass distributions for planets that could form around white dwarfs through CE evolution. We simulate populations of giant-planet systems, sampling initial conditions from observed mass and semi-major axis distributions for main sequence stars. We evolve the host star from main sequence to white dwarf to assess which planetary configurations could survive, and we predict the resulting post-CE planet population. Our results suggest that such planets should be rare, massive, and have very close orbital separations. We find that most of the surviving planets have masses of $>10\,M_{\rm{Jup}}$ and orbital separations $<1.4$ times the tidal disruption radius, $a_{disrupt}$ ($\lesssim0.006$ AU, also called the Roche limit), which is in contrast to high eccentricity migration, which produces planets with orbital separations $>2a_{disrupt}$. The properties of CE survivors from our simulations contrast with the known closely-orbiting planet WD 1856+534 b, suggesting a different mechanism may be responsible for its formation.

2610.27067.abstract: Collision-induced absorption (CIA) data are relevant to determining atmospheric temperatures and, in turn, the habitability of a diverse set of planetary atmospheres. However, these data remain sparse across broad wavelength and temperature ranges. Nevertheless, multiple, sometimes disagreeing, sources of experimental and theoretical data can be available for the same CIA pair. In this paper, we assess the impact of these varying sources on atmospheric temperatures and the limitations that the available data coverage can introduce. In order to inform future measurements and calculations, we test additional cases with extrapolated wavelength and temperature ranges. We first introduce a measure of the importance of CIA opacities depending on pressure and temperature by calculating the Rosseland mean with and without each CIA pair's contribution. Secondly, we employ each CIA source in a radiative transfer model of idealised atmospheres which maximise the effect of the CIA pair of interest. Our findings highlight the uncertainties related to the current data. Temperature differences between CIA data sources range from $\sim$10\,K when sources overlap in wavelength and temperature coverage to >100\,K when spectral gaps or temperature limits differ. Spectral windows or narrow temperature coverage can also hinder the model's convergence of the temperature profile. This work aims to provide guidance on the selection of CIA opacity datasets for atmospheric modelling and to identify the wavelength and temperature regimes in which further laboratory measurements and theoretical calculations are most urgently needed. We publish all our findings in detail in the form of an accessible website.

2610.27071.title: Beyond static torques: Self-consistent migration and dynamical trapping of low-mass planets in dusty disks

figures.caption:
Figure 1: Left and middle panels: relative surface density for the gas (left) and dust (middle) in the vicinity of a fixed planet after 50 orbits. Simulation parameters are $M_{p}=4\,M_{\oplus}$, $\text{St}=0.55$, $\epsilon=0.05$, $\alpha=10^{-3}$, and $\Sigma_{0}=5\times 10^{-3}\,M_{0}/r_{0}^{2}$. The upper and lower rows isolate the cases where turbulent diffusion and dust feedback are turned off and on, respectively. Notably, the trailing dust void and the over-dense streaming filament ahead of the planet are preserved in both scenarios.
Right panel: time evolution of the dimensionless migration rate, $\dot{a}/v_{\text{K}}$. The blue and red lines correspond to the fixed-orbit scenarios displayed in the left and middle panels, respectively, while the black line represents a self-consistent simulation in which turbulent dust diffusion and feedback are enabled and the planet dynamically migrates due to net torque from the disk (gas + dust)
(S48 in Table 2). The vertical dashed line marks the 50-orbit epoch of the density snapshots. The fixed simulation with diffusion and feedback turned off reproduces results comparable to those of [8]. While incorporating diffusion and feedback does not alter the overall direction of migration under fixed-orbit conditions, self-consistent migration noticeably modifies the migration rate, as evidenced by the departure between the red and black curves.

Figure 2: Evolution of the planet’s semi-major axis, $a_{\rm p}$, as a function of comoving time, $t^{\prime}/(2\pi)$, illustrating the three distinct deterministic migratory regimes. The bottom curve displays monotonic inward migration (S58 in Table B), driven primarily by the gas torque. The middle curve shows monotonic outward migration (S18 in Table B), resulting from a dominant positive dust torque. Finally, the top curve demonstrates oscillatory motion that results in radial confinement (S48 in Table B).

Figure 3: Time evolution of the planetary semi-major axis ($a/r_{0}$), showing a selected subset of migration regimes, mass bifurcation, and the emergence of multiple equilibrium zones. The panels isolate the effects of disk metallicity and initial orbital position ($a_{0}/r_{0}$). The top row corresponds to high-metallicity disks ($\epsilon=0.05$) and the bottom row to low-metallicity disks ($\epsilon=0.01$). Left and right columns separate initial positions $a_{0}/r_{0}=1$ and $a_{0}/r_{0}=10$, respectively. The reference simulation (S48: $M_{p}=4M_{\oplus}$, ${\rm St}=0.55$, $\epsilon=0.05$, $\alpha=10^{-3}$, high initial $\Sigma_{0}$) is indicated by the thick solid black line, demonstrating stable orbital trapping. Deviations from this baseline are encoded as follows: colors denote planetary mass (blue: $2.67M_{\oplus}$, black: $4M_{\oplus}$, red: $10M_{\oplus}$), line styles represent the Stokes number (solid: $\mathrm{St}=0.55$, dashed: $\mathrm{St}=0.26$, dashed-dot: ${\rm St}=0.1$), line thickness indicates initial gas surface density (thick: high $\Sigma_{0}$, thin: low $\Sigma_{0}$), and line transparency reflects turbulent viscosity (solid/dark lines: $\alpha=10^{-3}$, semi-transparent lines: $\alpha=10^{-4}$). The 28 simulations showed here are denoted with a dagger (†) in Table B.

Figure 4: Time evolution of the planetary semi-major axis normalized by its final time-averaged equilibrium value ($a_{\rm p}/a_{f}$) (top), dimensionless migration rate (middle), and eccentricity (bottom) for a $4M_{\oplus}$ planet in a highly viscous, metal-rich disk ($\alpha=10^{-3}$, $\epsilon=5.0\times 10^{-2}$, ${\rm St}=0.55$). A uniform filter was applied to the data in all three panels every 10 orbits. To demonstrate the universal scalability of the dynamical attractor, the curves have been phase-shifted. This shift and normalization explicitly reveals that, despite concurring at different absolute orbital distances and integration times, the dust-modulated traps converge into an identical oscillatory limit cycle. The vertical gray dotted lines, labeled $T_{1}$ through $T_{10}$, mark the exact comoving times ($t^{\prime}$) cross-sectioned in Figs. 6 and 7. These three simulations are indicated with gray rows in Table B.

Figure 5: Phase-space of the dynamical attractors corresponding to the simulations in Fig. 4. By mapping the dimensionless migration rate against the normalized semi-major axis, the emergence of distinct oscillatory limit cycles is clear. The blue and red regions highlight the stable confinement phases for the periods between 200–288 and 295–300 orbits, respectively. The sparse trajectories connecting these regions trace the dynamical transition as the planet shifts between equilibrium centers.

Figure 6: Temporal sequence of relative dust surface density maps ($\log_{10}(\Sigma_{\text{dust}}/\Sigma_{\text{dust},0})$), displayed across five representative phases of the limit cycle ($T_{6}$ through $T_{10}$), corresponding to the last five vertical dotted lines in Fig. 4, illustrating the hydrodynamic restoration of the dust trap during an inward-to-outward migration reversal for a $4\,M_{\oplus}$ planet. Both rows share identical disk parameters ($\alpha=10^{-3}$, $\epsilon=0.05$, $St=0.55$, and high $\Sigma_{0}$), differing only in their initial position. Top Row: A planet initialized at $a_{0}/r_{0}=10$ being captured after its initial inward migration. Bottom Row: A planet initialized at $a_{0}/r_{0}=1$ undergoing a similar bounce within the limit cycle. As the planet’s inward velocity slows, local conditions allow the solid material to replenish, dynamically restoring the sharp leading dust filament and trailing cavity. This cyclic restoration reactivates the strong positive torque necessary to halt inward decay.

Figure 7: Temporal sequence of relative dust surface density maps ($\log_{10}(\Sigma_{\text{dust}}/\Sigma_{\text{dust},0})$),
displayed across five representative phases of the limit cycle ($T_{1}$ through $T_{5}$), corresponding to the first five vertical dotted lines in Fig. 4, illustrating the dust structure during an outward-to-inward migration reversal within the trap for a $4\,M_{\oplus}$ planet. As in Fig. 6, both panels use the exact same disk setup, varying only the initial position. Top Row: A planet initialized at $a_{0}/r_{0}=10$ undergoing an outward-to-inward bounce. Bottom Row: A planet initialized at $a_{0}/r_{0}=1$ reaching the outer limit of its initial outward expansion.
During rapid outward migration, the planet’s orbital velocity outpaces the local hydrodynamic replenishment of the solid material. The leading dense filament gets weaker, causing the positive dust torque to be insufficient to counteract the negative gas torque, forcing the migration direction to reverse inward.

Figure 8: Left and middle panels: Relative surface density perturbations for the gas (left) and dust (middle) after 50 orbits. Simulation parameters are identical to those in Fig. 1. The rows isolate distinct physical mechanisms: dust feedback on, turbulent diffusion off (top), where the dust asymmetry is sharpest; dust feedback off and turbulent diffusion on with $\delta=\alpha$ (middle), where diffusion smooths the dust void and reduces the peak density of the leading filament, and the full model incorporating both feedback and turbulent diffusion (bottom). Comparing these panels reveals that dust feedback helps counteracting the effect of diffusion, maintaining a positive dust torque comparable to the lower viscosity case while keeping the negative gas torque lower in magnitude. Right panels: Time evolution of the torques normalized by $\Gamma_{\rm p}$ (see Eq. 4) for the dust (top) and gas (bottom). The inclusion of feedback (dash-dotted and red lines) consistently yields a higher positive dust torque and a less negative gas torque (closer to zero) compared to the case without feedback (dotted line), overall favoring outward migration.

2610.27071.abstract: The rapid inward migration of low-mass planets remains a primary theoretical challenge in planet formation. While recent studies show that the solid component of protoplanetary disks can exert strong positive torques to counteract the negative gas torques, traditional static fixed-orbit models fail to capture the fully coupled dynamics of a migrating planet. In this work, we present 2D high-resolution, two-fluid hydrodynamical simulations using a comoving reference frame to track the self-consistent orbital evolution of embedded planets across a comprehensive six-dimensional parameter space. By allowing the planet to dynamically respond to disk-exerted torques, we identify a wide diversity of migration regimes, involving inward/outward migration and oscillatory radial confinement. We also find that massive cores can overcome dust-induced barriers, experiencing dust-mediated runaway outward or inward migration. Conversely, in dust-rich environments continuous gas-dust momentum exchange combined with planet torques dynamically regenerates co-orbital dust asymmetries, creating robust dynamical attractors where super-Earths undergo stable, oscillatory confinement, effectively halting inward drift without requiring pre-existing pressure bumps or disk substructures. This self-induced trapping mechanism could be relevant in the outer disk, beyond the water-ice line in environments with a enhanced local dust-to-gas ratio, where icy pebbles are moderately coupled to the gas. In low-metallicity or highly diffusive disks, planets generally adopt monotonic inward decay, apart from cases with outward migration. Ultimately, the diversity of these self-consistent trajectories demonstrates that static torque approximations are insufficient. Evaluating fully coupled kinematic feedback is essential for accurately predicting planetary survival and the final architecture of planetary systems.

2610.27136.title: Ammonia-Hydrogen Phase Equilibria in Planetary Envelopes from First-Principles-Based Machine-Learning Molecular Dynamics

2610.27136.abstract: Ammonia and hydrogen are major constituents of planets within and beyond the solar system, yet how they interact in planetary envelopes is poorly known. We perform large-scale two-phase coexistence simulations of the ammonia-hydrogen system from 500 to 4000 K and 0.1 to 100 GPa, driven by machine-learning interatomic potentials trained on density functional theory calculations. From these we map the compositions of coexisting hydrogen-rich and ammonia-rich phases, and the critical curve that separates conditions of complete miscibility from those of phase separation. The critical temperature increases with pressure, from 500 K at 0.1 GPa to 2000 K near 30 GPa, and we find no phase separation at 3000 and 4000 K up to 100 GPa. The slope of the critical curve decreases substantially between 0.3 and 30 GPa, and the curve nearly flattens above about 30 GPa and 2000 K, where molecules begin to give way to atomic species. The coexistence curves are asymmetric with an ammonia-rich critical composition. For the expected envelope compositions, the phase boundary lies close to, and intersects, published thermal profiles of Uranus and Neptune, implying ammonia may be raining out in these planets today. In contrast, in warm sub-Neptunes such as TOI-270 d, ammonia and hydrogen are likely miscible in all proportions. Together with previous studies, our results suggest that silicates, water and ammonia separate from hydrogen in sequence as planets cool, with implications for their compositional, thermal and structural evolution.

2610.27197.title: Analytical Chemistry at the Planetary Frontier

2610.27197.abstract: Planetary science depends on chemical measurements made under conditions very different from those in a terrestrial laboratory. This review treats the analytical methods of planetary science as one connected chain, from orbital remote sensing through in-situ measurements by landers and rovers and sample collection and curation, to the micro-analysis of returned material on Earth. Orbital methods, including visible and near-infrared reflectance, thermal emission and gamma-ray and neutron spectroscopy, are discussed first. In-situ techniques are then reviewed, including laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS), micro-focus X-ray fluorescence (XRF), deep-ultraviolet Raman and fluorescence spectroscopy, evolved gas analysis with gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) and miniaturized mass spectrometry. Contamination control and curation practices are described, followed by laboratory techniques such as secondary ion mass spectrometry (SIMS and NanoSIMS), atom probe tomography (APT), thermal ionization mass spectrometry (TIMS), synchrotron micro-XRF and X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) spectroscopy. Accuracy, calibration and reference materials are discussed as the link between in-situ and laboratory data, and the role of chemometrics and data fusion is examined. Flight and laboratory instruments are compared in terms of spatial resolution, detection limit, sample consumption and throughput. Active neutron-gamma spectroscopy planned for the Dragonfly mission to Titan is also discussed. This comparison shows that in-situ and laboratory techniques are complementary. In-situ instruments provide context and select samples, while laboratory techniques provide isotopic, molecular and speciation data that cannot yet be obtained in situ.

2610.27453.abstract:
Context. A multi-chord stellar occultation by (1201) Strenua observed on 26 April 2026 is combined with ATLAS $c$- and $o$-band photometry.
Aims. We aim to determine the size and geometric albedo of Strenua and reassess its taxonomic classification.
Methods. Four positive chords from a 47-station campaign across Indonesia were fitted within a Bayesian forward-modeling framework to derive an ellipse cross-section and equivalent diameter. ATLAS photometry was modeled using the $H, G_1, G_2$ phase-function system to determine band-specific absolute magnitudes, converted to $H_{\mathrm{V}}$, and combined with the occultation diameter to calculate geometric albedo and update taxonomy.
Results. The chords yield semi-axes $a' = 27.49^{+3.90}_{-1.65}$~km and $b' = 14.33^{+2.37}_{-2.69}$~km (position angle $95.3^{+4.9}_{-2.7}$ deg), giving an area-equivalent diameter $D_{\mathrm{eq}} = 39.86^{+2.06}_{-1.66}$~km. Photometric modeling gives $H_c = 11.50 \pm 0.05$~mag ($G_{1,c} = 0.81 \pm 0.08$, $G_{2,c} = 0.04 \pm 0.02$) and $H_o = 11.29^{+0.02}_{-0.03}$~mag ($G_{1,o} = 0.94^{+0.03}_{-0.05}$, $G_{2,o} = 0.01 \pm 0.01$), yielding $H_{\mathrm{V}} = 11.46 \pm 0.05$~mag. The resulting geometric albedo $p_{\mathrm{V}} = 0.029 \pm 0.003$ places Strenua among the darkest primitive asteroids, securely reclassifying it as P-class and resolving its legacy X-complex ambiguity.

2610.27484.abstract: The survival of exomoons around close-in white dwarf planets offers a potential constraint on their migration histories and an alternative pathway to post-main-sequence habitability. We investigate whether moons can survive the tidal circularization of planets via high-eccentricity migration, and consider a hierarchical three-body system (white dwarf-planet-moon) after an initial eccentricity excitation of the planetary orbit. Using an analytic equilibrium tidal model, we compare the evolution of the planetary and satellite orbits and examine the conditions required for an evection resonance. We show that the moons of pseudosynchronously rotating planets always migrate inwards since the planetary corotation radius always exceeds the Hill radius, independent of mass and orbital eccentricities. Comparing the migration timescales for the moon and the planet shows that compact moons undergo rapid tidal decay relative to the outer orbit. However, the wider separations favored by slower migration timescales experience pericenter perturbations whose work constitutes a substantial fraction of the moon's orbital energy. Together, our results indicate that moons likely do not survive during a planet's high-eccentricity migration phase in a three-body configuration.

2610.27788.abstract: The initial volatile element inventories in a planet's atmosphere, mantle, and core are established by delivery and transport during planetary growth. Conversely, the volatile abundances of Earth's planetary reservoirs record its accretion pathway. We model here volatile transport during planet formation for two different delivery scenarios, via pebble and planetesimal accretion, to predict the volatile inventories of proto-Earth at the end of its main accretion phase. We find that the distributions of volatiles between the atmosphere, mantle, and core exhibit strong sensitivity to volatile delivery timing, metal-silicate partition coefficients, atmosphere-magma solubilities, and planet mass. In particular, the early volatile delivery expected in pebble accretion scenarios substantially enhances core sequestration of hydrogen and carbon relative to continuous delivery during incremental planetesimal accretion. With our fiducial partition coefficients, the pebble accretion model produces a 760 bar carbon-dominated atmosphere with 39 bar of hydrogen and water and a few bars of nitrogen, consistent with volatile concentration estimates for bulk silicate Earth including the atmosphere. The corresponding planetesimal accretion model produces a more massive ($\sim$$1350$ bar) atmosphere with similar composition. The core stores $\sim$$70$% of both the H and the C budget in the early-delivery scenario, but $\lesssim$$50$% in the corresponding continuous delivery scenario. Overall our results demonstrate that substantial amounts of volatiles are sequestered into rocky planet cores during planet formation and that the volatile inventory of bulk silicate Earth was likely established already during the magma ocean phase of planet formation.

2610.28117.abstract: Observations of exoplanetary atmospheres have revealed a rather complex co-existence between the gaseous and condensed phases, ranging from atmospheres apparently covered in clouds to clear ones, across a myriad of intermediate regimes. The interaction between solids and stellar radiation is of fundamental importance when forward or retrieval models are compared to observations. The simplest approach is to assume spherical particles, whose scattering and absorption properties are readily computed with Mie theory. More advanced computational methods, however, can also treat non-spherical condensates. Among these, the transition matrix approach has proven to provide a rigorous and efficient calculation of the extinction by non-spherical particles over a broad range of sizes and refractive indices. We here focus on the absorption and scattering cross sections of forsterite, spinel and silicon monoxide from the near to the far infrared range for particles of different sizes, with shapes ranging from compact ensembles of spheres to porous aggregates. We find that, depending on the size and the configuration chosen, the differences in extinction can be as high as a factor of 2-3, with structured grains being more efficient absorbers in the near infrared for sizes greater than 1 $\mu$m. In a fiducial transmission spectrum we show that in the $\lambda = 1-5\,\mu$m range the amount of spherical material needed to match the contribution of the structured grains can be a factor 2 higher. Such calculations, available for the community through a Zenodo repository, prove to be useful for interpreting recent and future observations of exoplanetary atmospheres.

2610.28518.abstract: The TESS mission is designed to survey the entire sky to find planets most amenable to follow-up observations, and transit searches have therefore focused specifically on bright targets. Faint stars ($T_{mag}>13.5$) have not been systematically searched for planets, despite TESS having the sensitivity necessary to do so, therefore representing a promising avenue for increasing TESS's scientific yield. We utilized TESS's sensitivity for faint stars in particular to find more planets for joint optical-UV studies of exoplanet transits. Observing transits in both UV and optical gives insight into exoplanet atmosphere composition and evolution and remains relatively unexplored due to the lack of UV-capable instruments. ULTRASAT is an upcoming UV space telescope that will perform a high cadence survey suitable for observing exoplanet transits. To increase the sample size of planets capable of observations with ULTRASAT, we performed a transit search of faint stars down to $T_{mag}=16$ in the ULTRASAT high cadence survey fields using TESS light curves optimized for faint stars. Our search recovered 262 planet candidates, of which 181 are new to this work. We also statistically validated 2 of those candidates as bona fide planets. Finally, we estimated the ULTRASAT SNR of both new and existing planet candidates, and found that 113 targets will be detectable with ULTRASAT, which would facilitate the largest study of transiting planets in the visible and UV. This work demonstrates the power of TESS to detect exoplanets around faint stars and provides a catalog of well-vetted transiting planet candidates to observe with ULTRASAT.

2610.28533.abstract: Hot Jupiters are typically thought to be "lonely", but a small and growing subset of them have been found to have nearby planets in the same system. We present the discovery of a new member of this class of systems, TOI-3686. TOI-3686 c is a hot Jupiter with $P_\mathrm{orb} = 5.078$ days detected by NASA's TESS mission that shows peak-to-peak transit timing variations (TTVs) of 40 minutes, amongst the largest ever observed for a hot Jupiter. A subsequent search of the TESS data revealed the transits of a second planet, TOI-3686 b, a sub-Neptune with $P_\mathrm{orb} = 2.54$~days and peak-to-peak TTVs of 10 hours, $\sim 16\%$ of its orbital period. We characterized the system through photodynamical modeling of photometry from TESS and ground-based facilities, as well as radial velocity measurements from the NEID and MAROON-X spectrographs. We find that the two planets in the TOI-3686 system are deep in a 2:1 mean-motion resonance, making this the only hot Jupiter system currently known to be in a truly resonant configuration, which may be related to its $\lesssim1$~Gyr system age. Systems like TOI-3686 likely formed through a dynamically quiescent pathway and were captured into resonance after migration through a disk, and may represent the high-mass end of processes that occur in compact systems of smaller planets.

2610.28575.abstract: Small planets transiting the nearest M dwarfs are the terrestrial planets most accessible to detailed characterisation. We report a sub-Earth-sized transiting planet candidate in the wide (17.6") M-dwarf binary GJ 774 at 12.86 pc, most likely orbiting the M2.5 primary GJ 774 A (TIC 351339274). The signal was a SPOC multi-sector threshold-crossing event (MES = 7.95) and is not a TESS Object of Interest. In eight TESS sectors (2019-2026) a 1.28-h transit recurs every 4.225138 +/- 0.000010 d with a box-mean depth of 365 +/- 32 ppm in A's light. The 2026 data, which entered neither the SPOC search nor our selection, show it at the ephemeris predicted from 2019-2023 data (304 +/- 43 ppm; none of 10^5 phase-scrambled versions of the 2026 data is as deep). The per-target false-alarm probability is < 0.03 at 95%. Odd/even, secondary-eclipse, archival-plate and Gaia radial-velocity tests exclude unrelated blended eclipsing binaries and eclipsing companions on 4.2-d orbits, and hierarchical eclipsing binaries are improbable. The stars are 0.85 TESS pixel apart, so the TRICERATOPS false-positive probability (0.26) is set by a planet on GJ 774 B. B is disfavoured because its own light does not dim enough: PRF-deblended photometry gives 109 +/- 115 ppm in B's light, against 1089 ppm required if B were the host. Conditional on a point source at A or at B, the joint host model gives P(A)=0.59-0.97 (0.97 for the native target-pixel baseline). Over all sectors the PRF photometry is consistent with A, but in the out-of-sample 2026 data 40% of the deficit appears at B's position, an unexplained 2-3 sigma (PSF-model and depth dependent) tension with host A. On A the planet has R_p=0.70 +/- 0.06 R_Earth, S=15.0 +/- 1.8 S_Earth and T_eq=548 +/- 16 K. It is not validated; resolved ground-based photometry of the pair would test host B directly.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Microlensed oscillating source. The three coloured disks show the source star at different positions as its line of sight passes close to that of a lensing object. The gray dot shows the projected position of the lens, and the thin lines correspond to equal lens magnification strengths. Exaggerated bright and dark surface regions on the disks illustrate the local flux perturbations caused by stellar oscillations. As the lens and source approach each other in projection, the magnification varies across the stellar disk and weights different parts of the mode pattern unequally. Even when the disks overlap in projection, the source is not occulted. Light is deflected to angles of order the Einstein radius, far beyond the physical disk of the lens, so close approaches produce magnification rather than shadowing.

From left to right, the lens moves from a large separation ($u=1000\,\rho_{s}$) to a close transit ($u=0.5\,\rho_{s}$). 2610.28005.abstract: Asteroseismology relies on disk-integrated photometry or radial velocities, in which geometric cancellation suppresses modes of high spherical degree ($l\geq4$). Observations are thus limited to deeply penetrating, low-degree modes, leaving the outer envelope inaccessible. We investigate whether a high-magnification microlensing event can temporarily lift this limitation by differentially magnifying the surface of an oscillating source star. We modelled the visibility of solar-like oscillations during microlensing, weighting the surface by limb darkening and the local magnification. We computed multiplet visibilities and the power distribution among azimuthal components, and built a likelihood model for recovering the 3D spin-axis orientation from resolved rotational multiplets. When the lens-source separation becomes comparable to the source's angular radius, the magnification gradient acts as a transient spatial filter that breaks the symmetry of disk integration, raising high-degree mode visibilities by up to three orders of magnitude. The same non-axisymmetric weighting makes the relative power of azimuthal components depend on both the inclination and sky-projected azimuth of the spin axis, imprinting the full spin orientation onto the power spectrum. With $5\%$ relative-power uncertainties, we recover the orientation to $\sigma_i=2.9^\circ$ and $\sigma_\gamma=11.5^\circ$. Microlensing thus does more than amplify distant stars: its magnification pattern enables spatially selective asteroseismology. The effect is strongest for rare close encounters and unlikely to support large samples, and the newly visible high-degree modes will overlap with rotationally split and mixed modes, complicating mode identification. Nevertheless, individual high-quality events may open a window on envelope physics and spin geometries for stars in the Galactic bulge and beyond.

2610.28331.abstract: Massive protostellar disks are expected to sustain high accretion rates through gravitational instability, while dust growth may modify their opacity, cooling efficiency, and stability. Conversely, the time-dependent and nonaxisymmetric structures produced by gravitational instability may regulate the local conditions for dust growth. However, the coupled evolution of dust growth and gravitational instability in massive protostellar disks has not yet been explored self-consistently. We present two-dimensional hydrodynamic simulations that follow gas dynamics, dust growth, and opacity-dependent radiative cooling in a massive protostellar disk. We find that dust grains rapidly grow to millimeter-centimeter sizes shortly after disk formation, substantially reducing the infrared opacity. The enhanced cooling promotes disk fragmentation and produces more frequent accretion-driven luminosity outbursts than in a model without dust growth, with durations and peak luminosities comparable to those observed in massive protostars. Dust growth is broadly regulated by the fragmentation-limited size in dense disk regions, whereas newly formed outer disk regions and low-density regions deviate from this limit because of finite collision timescales and dust transport. These results suggest that dust growth may facilitate episodic accretion and fragmentation, while gravitationally unstable disk structures in turn regulate the dust growth process.

2610.28345.abstract: Age is the one of the most difficult stellar properties to constrain. However, upcoming surveys such as PLATO are about to revolutionize our ability to measure FGK dwarf ages with asteroseismology. Here, we use The Cannon to construct a data-driven model for inferring asteroseismic-quality age measurements from large spectroscopic survey observations and demonstrate that forthcoming asteroseismology datasets from future surveys can be leveraged, together with our model, to obtain stellar age samples larger than can be obtained by those surveys alone. We train The Cannon on 323 FGK dwarf stars with asteroseismic age labels from NASA Kepler photometry and high-resolution spectra from the Apache Point Observatory Galactic Evolution Experiment (APOGEE). We apply our model to FGK dwarfs from the Kepler survey that exhibit solar-like oscillations and reproduce their reported asteroseismic-quality ages with an RMS scatter of 1.0 Gyr. We then apply our model to the sample of 3810 Kepler FGK dwarfs with APOGEE spectra to infer data-driven asteroseismic ages. We repeat this for the larger sample of 48,828 FGK dwarfs with APOGEE spectra. Our work demonstrates that data-driven methods can robustly reproduce asteroseismic ages for FGK dwarfs. These methods will be invaluable tools for extending asteroseimology measurements from upcoming surveys (e.g., PLATO) to much larger stellar samples.

2610.28485.title: A Solar Optical Clock

figures.caption: Figure 1: Comparison of a grating-based astrophysical spectrometer to a laser heterodyne spectrometer designed in analogy to a modern optical clock. (a) Conceptual layout of a direct-detection grating spectrograph. The dispersed stellar spectrum is measured on a detector array, and Doppler shifts are determined by averaging the wavelength shifts of many lines across the stellar spectrum. (b) Schematic of a solar optical clock. A probe laser is locked to the center of a transition in the solar spectrum using heterodyne spectroscopy and modulation techniques. The frequency of the probe laser is simultaneously measured relative to an optical frequency comb. The resulting frequency measurements encode Doppler velocity information that can be used to probe phenomena related to exoplanets, solar physics, and atmospheric science.

Figure 2: Overview of our experimental approach. Sunlight is coupled into single-mode optical fiber and mixed with a local oscillator (LO) laser on a photodetector. The resulting heterodyne signal is measured within a defined radio-frequency bandwidth ($b$) and passed to a power detection and rectification circuit. Frequency modulation of the LO laser and lock-in detection of the heterodyne signal power generate an error signal with a zero crossing at the center of the solar line. A loop filter locks the LO to the zero crossing, and the frequency of the stabilized LO laser is simultaneously measured against an optical frequency comb.

Figure 3: (a) Sweeping the LO frequency reveals the solar iron line at 1565.28 nm. (b) The 1st-order error signal with a zero crossing at the center of the line. (c) Theoretical sensitivity vs. FM dither amplitude, assuming a total quantum efficiency of $\eta_{tot}\approx 0.7$ and a mean photon occupancy of $\langle n\rangle\approx 0.25$ photons/s-Hz. The solid lines show the change in sensitivity for 1st-order lock-in detection with different integrated optical bandwidths $\Deltau$, and the dashed and dotted lines show the change in sensitivity with 3rd-order lock-in detection and square-wave lock-in detection respectively.

Figure 4: Comparison of FM-locked and swept LHR. (a) Frequency shifts observed over 5000 seconds of continuous measurements. The SNR-efficient FM LHR (dark blue) reaches a higher precision in a shorter amount of time than swept LHR (light blue). A small drift is present due to coupling between the apparent orientation of the Sun’s rotational axis and a slight asymmetry in the antenna pattern of the light collection optics. Binning of the FM data to 100 s intervals yields the smoothed grey line. (b) The power spectral density (PSD) of these binned data clearly reveals the 5.5 min oscillation period characteristic of solar p-modes. (c) The Allan deviations of the FM and swept LHR data. Again, evidence of solar p-modes is present for the FM data, which shows a peak in the averaging time at half the p-mode period ($\sim$ 150 s). The dotted lines represent the Allan deviation after linearly detrending the frequency shifts, and the dashed line indicates the theoretical quantum-limit for FM-locked LHR sensitivity discussed in Section 3 and derived analytically in the Appendix.

2610.28485.abstract: Precision spectroscopy underpins quantum sensing, atomic timekeeping, and the search for terrestrial-mass exoplanets. Finding an Earth-Sun analog requires fractional splitting of spectral features that rivals the precision of the best laboratory spectroscopy. This corresponds to resolution of a few parts in $10^5$ of a typical stellar spectral line, or a Doppler velocity precision of less than 10 cm s$^{-1}$. Only a few astrophysical spectrometers reach this regime, and only by dispersing starlight with large gratings and averaging thousands of lines. Here, we show that comparable precision can be achieved on a single solar line by leveraging techniques used in quantum sensors and optical clocks. A laser is frequency-locked to the 1565 nm solar Fe I line by coupling to a single mode of the solar thermal field and counted against an optical frequency comb referenced to the SI second, thus creating a solar optical clock. Operating at the fundamental photon-noise limit of thermal heterodyne spectroscopy, we achieve centroid precision of one part in $10^9$ of the optical frequency, or 30 cm s$^{-1}$ in radial velocity. We recover the Sun's five-minute acoustic oscillations and the expected Rossiter-McLaughlin signal during a solar eclipse. Combining these techniques from quantum sensing with a thirty-meter-class telescope could enable our demonstrated precision on the nearest Sun-like stars in a few hours. Multiplexing such absolute frequency measurements across lines with different magnetic sensitivity and formation depth would reduce averaging time and help disentangle stellar granulation and activity from the Doppler signature of terrestrial exoplanets, providing new approaches to address some of the most demanding measurements in astrophysical spectroscopy.

2610.28603.abstract: Solar energetic particle (SEP) events threaten space infrastructure, yet physics-based prediction models depend on numerous poorly constrained free parameters. We introduce the Fujitsu Solar Energetic particle Intelligent Tuning and Evaluation Network (SEITEN), which couples the SUSANOO MHD model of CME propagation to SEPIF, a diffusive shock acceleration and focused transport model, through the shock conditions SUSANOO supplies, and automatically optimizes the free parameters of the particle model against the SEP event of 9 October 2021. The mean free path and the injection efficiency vary independently along each magnetic field line and heliolongitudinal bin, giving a 19-dimensional problem solved by quasi-Monte Carlo sampling followed by a Tree-structured Parzen Estimator. The optimized model reproduces proton flux profiles at five spacecraft with a mean absolute error of $\approx 0.45$ in $\log_{10}$ flux, and the inferred mean free paths show a clear east-west structure; these are effective parameters conditional on the assumed transport geometry. Six independent runs show that whether mean free paths or injection efficiencies dominate depends on the MHD shock strength, and that injection efficiencies differ by orders of magnitude between MHD configurations despite nearly identical fit quality. Joint MHD-SEP parameter estimation is therefore a necessary next step towards generalized, operational SEP forecasting.
